events.title: Challenger is lost
events.description: Seven people die when the shuttle breaks apart after launch. NASA pauses flights and investigates.

events.title: Black Monday hits markets
events.description: The Dow falls 22.6% in one day. The monthly chart combines that day with all the other trading days in October.

events.title: The Berlin Wall opens
events.description: East Germans begin crossing the border freely. The change becomes a powerful symbol of a changing Europe.

events.title: Hubble launches into orbit
events.description: The space telescope leaves Earth aboard Discovery. Its first images later reveal a flaw in the main mirror.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple and Coca-Cola finished close together at the top of this set, while IBM ended only slightly higher than it began. With the same $10,000 start, Coca-Cola reached about $38,700 and IBM about $10,300. All three were familiar companies, but their investment results were far apart.

Apple introduced the color-capable Macintosh II in 1987, and IBM’s new PS/2 line sold more than a million units in its first year. Coca-Cola’s board approved the sale of its Columbia Pictures stake to Sony in 1989 and said it expected an after-tax gain of about $530 million. Those examples show very different company choices; they cannot alone explain the stock results.

The share baskets gained overall, but neither matched the leading individual companies. They also did not depend on one company succeeding. That is a trade-off: spreading money around can mean missing a spectacular winner's full gain while reducing dependence on one business.

The final ranking was not available in September 1985. Nor could an investor know when the large market fall would arrive. The outcome is clear now because the whole five-year path has already happened.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Apple’s leadership split, Coca-Cola’s formula reversal and plans for a weaker dollar all attracted attention.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Different companies followed very different paths. Size and reputation did not guarantee high returns, and a bad headline did not settle a company’s future.
reflection.what_faded_away: The immediate tax-bill timetable and the first reactions to a new musical did not determine the final ranking.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: No starting headline revealed that Apple and Coca-Cola would end so close together. Their past difficulties were clues to consider, not a ready-made answer.

hot:1985-09:apple.text: Apple introduced the Macintosh II on March 2, 1987, adding support for color displays to its Mac line. Customers could choose a Mac with color graphics; Apple shares rose over this five-year window.

hot:1985-09:coca-cola.text: In 1989, Coca-Cola’s board approved the sale of its Columbia Pictures stake to Sony. Coke said it expected an after-tax gain of about $530 million; soft drinks remained its main business, and its shares finished higher.

hot:1985-09:ibm.text: IBM announced its PS/2 line in April 1987 and reported more than one million sold by November. Those sales showed buyers were taking up the new computer family; IBM shares ended slightly higher during this window.
